did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to eat the scroll and then go and speak to the house of Israel. Eating the scroll symbolizes accepting and internalizing God’s word before delivering it to others.

Did you know? Although the content of his mission is difficult, Ezekiel describes the scroll as tasting sweet as honey in his mouth. The sweetness refers to accepting and internalizing God’s word, not necessarily to the difficult content of the prophecy.

Did you know? God makes clear to Ezekiel that he is being sent to the house of Israel, not to a people who speak a foreign language. The main difficulty of his mission is not a language barrier but the people’s refusal to listen.

Did you know? The house of Israel is described as “stubborn and hardhearted” because it is unwilling to listen to God. This description emphasizes the people’s obstinacy and the challenge awaiting the prophet.

Did you know? God promises to make Ezekiel’s forehead strong against the people, “as hard as flint, harder than stone.” The image expresses steadfastness and courage in the face of opposition, and immediately afterward he is told not to fear or be dismayed.

Did you know? When the spirit lifts Ezekiel up, he hears a great rumbling sound behind him, including the declaration: “Blessed is the glory of the LORD from His place.” The vision connects the movement of the spirit with the revelation of God’s glory.

Did you know? Ezekiel comes to the exiles in Tel-abib, who are living beside the Kebar River, and remains there for seven days, “stunned” among them. Before beginning his public ministry, he goes through a period of silence and astonishment.

Did you know? Ezekiel is appointed as a “watchman” for the house of Israel. His role is to hear the word from God and warn the people in His name, even though there is no guarantee that those who hear will accept the warning.

Did you know? The chapter emphasizes the prophet’s responsibility to warn the wicked: if he fails to warn him, the prophet will be held accountable for not delivering God’s word. Nevertheless, the wicked person himself will die for his sin.

Did you know? The righteous person also must be warned if he is in danger of sinning. When Ezekiel warns him and he refrains from sin, the righteous person will live, and Ezekiel will have saved his life.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Ezekiel is not free to speak as he wishes: when God speaks to him, his mouth will be opened and he will deliver God’s words. The concluding message is: “Let those who hear, hear; and let those who refuse, refuse.”
